questions.q: Which long bone of the upper limb is the first bone to begin ossifying in the fetus and ossifies partly via intramembranous ossification?
questions.explain: The clavicle begins ossifying in the fifth to sixth fetal week, primarily through intramembranous ossification of its medial and lateral shaft before endochondral ossification contributes to its ends. Most other long bones ossify purely by endochondral ossification.

open.q: Which upper limb bone is the first to begin ossifying in utero and ossifies largely by intramembranous ossification?

questions.q: On which surface of the scapula is the deep subscapular fossa located?
questions.explain: The costal (anterior) surface of the scapula faces the thoracic cage and contains the concave subscapular fossa, which serves as the origin of subscapularis. The scapular spine divides the posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.

open.q: Which surface of the scapula contains the subscapular fossa?

questions.q: Which groove on the humeral shaft lodges the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery as they wind around the back of the humerus?
questions.explain: The radial (spiral) groove runs obliquely across the posterior surface of the humerus between the lateral and medial heads of triceps brachii, carrying the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery. Mid-shaft humeral fractures can injure these structures.

open.q: Which groove on the posterior humerus contains the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery?

questions.q: Which prominent bony feature at the proximal end of the ulna forms the point of the elbow and receives the triceps brachii tendon?
questions.explain: The olecranon is the large proximal projection of the ulna that fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus during elbow extension and serves as the insertion site for triceps brachii. The coronoid process lies anteriorly below the trochlear notch.

open.q: Which proximal ulnar projection forms the prominence of the elbow and receives triceps brachii?

questions.q: Which carpal bone of the proximal row is most commonly fractured after a fall onto an outstretched hand, risking avascular necrosis of its proximal pole?
questions.explain: The scaphoid lies across both proximal and distal carpal rows and is vulnerable to fracture on a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH). Its retrograde blood supply enters distally, making the proximal pole prone to avascular necrosis or non-union.

open.q: Which carpal bone is most frequently fractured after a fall onto an outstretched hand and can develop proximal pole avascular necrosis?

questions.q: Why does a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus place the axillary nerve at risk?
options: The axillary nerve passes directly through the olecranon fossa
The axillary nerve winds closely around the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral artery
The axillary nerve lies inside the carpal tunnel
The axillary nerve pierces the medial epicondyle
questions.explain: After passing through the quadrangular space, the axillary nerve wraps posteriorly around the surgical neck of the humerus alongside the posterior circumflex humeral artery. Surgical neck fractures or anterior shoulder dislocations can injure it.

open.q: Why can a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus injure the axillary nerve?
accept: the axillary nerve winds closely around the surgical neck
it courses directly against the surgical neck
the nerve wraps around the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral artery
it lies in close anatomical contact with the surgical neck

questions.q: Which bony landmark on the medial side of the distal humerus is directly related to the ulnar nerve behind the elbow?
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus in the cubital tunnel/ulnar groove, making it palpable and susceptible to injury at the elbow or in medial epicondyle fractures.

open.q: Behind which humeral prominence does the ulnar nerve pass at the elbow?

questions.q: Which muscle forms the bulk of the anterior chest wall and adducts and medially rotates the humerus?
questions.explain: Pectoralis major is a large fan-shaped muscle of the anterior chest wall that adducts, medially rotates, and (via its clavicular head) flexes the humerus. Pectoralis minor lies deep to it and attaches to the coracoid process.

open.q: Which large anterior chest muscle adducts and medially rotates the humerus?

questions.q: Damage to the long thoracic nerve during axillary surgery leads to paralysis of serratus anterior and causes which characteristic clinical sign?
questions.explain: Serratus anterior holds the medial border of the scapula against the thoracic wall and protracts/rotates the scapula during overhead arm elevation. Paralysis from long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula, especially when pushing forward or raising the arm.

open.q: What clinical sign results from paralysis of serratus anterior due to long thoracic nerve injury?

questions.q: Approximately what proportion of lymph from the mammary gland (breast) drains into the axillary lymph nodes?
options: None, it drains only to popliteal nodes
questions.explain: Roughly 75% of breast lymph drains toward the axillary lymph nodes (especially from the lateral quadrants), while much of the remainder drains to parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes. Axillary nodes are a key route for breast cancer spread and staging.

open.q: Approximately what percentage of lymphatic drainage from the breast goes to the axillary lymph nodes?

questions.q: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the axilla?
options: Subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi
First rib, outer border of rib 1, and clavicle
questions.explain: The anterior axillary wall is formed primarily by pectoralis major and pectoralis minor (along with clavipectoral fascia). The posterior wall is formed by subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi.

open.q: Which muscles form the anterior wall of the axilla?

questions.q: Which roots of the spinal nerves typically form the brachial plexus?
questions.explain: The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1, supplying motor and sensory innervation to the upper limb. C1 to C4 form the cervical plexus.

open.q: Which spinal nerve roots form the brachial plexus?

questions.q: Which terminal branch of the brachial plexus arises from the lateral and medial cords and supplies most flexors of the forearm and intrinsic muscles of the thenar eminence?
questions.explain: The median nerve is formed by contributions from the lateral and medial cords (C5 to T1) and innervates most anterior forearm flexors (except flexor carpi ulnaris and medial flexor digitorum profundus) plus the thenar muscles and lateral two lumbricals.

open.q: Which major nerve of the upper limb is formed by the lateral and medial cords and supplies most forearm flexors and thenar muscles?

questions.q: A newborn delivered with difficult shoulder dystocia has traction injury to the upper trunk (C5 to C6) of the brachial plexus, resulting in an adducted, medially rotated arm and extended pronated forearm. What is this pattern called?
questions.explain: Erb-Duchenne palsy involves C5 to C6 (upper trunk) injury, paralyzing abductors/lateral rotators of the shoulder (deltoid, supraspinatus) and elbow flexors/supinators (biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis), giving the classic waiter's tip posture. Klumpke palsy affects C8 to T1 (lower trunk).

open.q: What palsy results from upper brachial plexus (C5 to C6) injury and produces an adducted, medially rotated arm with extended forearm?

questions.q: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the axillary nerve and radial nerve?
questions.explain: The posterior cord of the brachial plexus divides into the axillary nerve (C5 to C6) and the radial nerve (C5 to T1), supplying posterior compartment muscles of the arm and forearm along with associated skin.

open.q: From which cord of the brachial plexus do the axillary and radial nerves originate?

questions.q: Which four muscles constitute the rotator cuff (SITS) of the shoulder joint?
options: Deltoid, teres major, latissimus dorsi, and pectoralis major
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis
Coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, brachialis, and triceps brachii
Rhomboid major, rhomboid minor, levator scapulae, and trapezius
questions.explain: The rotator cuff comprises supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis, whose tendons blend with the fibrous capsule of the glenohumeral joint to dynamically stabilize the humeral head.

open.q: Which four muscles form the rotator cuff of the shoulder?
accept: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis

questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle is primarily responsible for initiating abduction of the arm at the glenohumeral joint (roughly the first 15 degrees)?
questions.explain: Supraspinatus (supplied by the suprascapular nerve) initiates shoulder abduction for the first ~15 degrees before the deltoid gains mechanical advantage. Subscapularis medially rotates, while infraspinatus and teres minor laterally rotate.

open.q: Which rotator cuff muscle initiates abduction of the arm at the shoulder joint?

questions.q: Which structures pass through the quadrangular space of the posterior scapular/axillary region?
options: Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Suprascapular nerve and transverse cervical artery
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
questions.explain: The quadrangular space is bounded by teres minor superiorly, teres major inferiorly, long head of triceps medially, and surgical neck of the humerus laterally, transmitting the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery.

open.q: Which nerve and artery pass through the quadrangular space?
accept: axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
axillary nerve with posterior circumflex humeral artery

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the three muscles of the anterior (flexor) compartment of the arm: biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis?
questions.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5 to C7) pierces coracobrachialis and supplies coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis in the anterior arm compartment, continuing distally as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm?

questions.q: Why does brachialis remain an effective elbow flexor even when the forearm is pronated, whereas biceps brachii loses much of its supination-linked mechanical advantage?
options: Brachialis inserts onto the radius and rotates the forearm
Brachialis inserts directly onto the ulna (coronoid process/tuberosity) regardless of forearm rotation
Brachialis is innervated by the femoral nerve
Biceps brachii originates from the patella
questions.explain: Brachialis crosses only the elbow joint and inserts onto the ulna, flexing the elbow efficiently in any forearm position. Biceps brachii inserts onto the radial tuberosity and acts as both a powerful supinator of a flexed forearm and an elbow flexor.

open.q: Why does brachialis flex the elbow effectively regardless of forearm rotation?
accept: it inserts onto the ulna rather than the rotating radius
its ulnar insertion is unaffected by pronation or supination
it attaches to the ulna across the elbow

questions.q: Which muscle forms the sole or primary muscle of the posterior (extensor) compartment of the arm and is supplied by the radial nerve?
questions.explain: Triceps brachii (long, lateral, and medial heads) occupies the posterior compartment of the arm and extends the elbow, receiving innervation from the radial nerve.

open.q: Which muscle occupies the posterior compartment of the arm and extends the elbow?

questions.q: From lateral to medial, what are the main neurovascular contents within the cubital fossa?
options: Ulnar nerve, brachial artery, and radial nerve
Median nerve, radial nerve, and ulnar artery
Brachial vein, ulnar artery, and musculocutaneous nerve
Radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, and median nerve
questions.explain: Within the cubital fossa (bounded superiorly by an interepicondylar line, laterally by brachioradialis, and medially by pronator teres), the structures from lateral to medial are the radial nerve (deep/lateral), tendon of biceps brachii, brachial artery, and median nerve.

open.q: List the main structures in the cubital fossa from lateral to medial.
accept: radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, and median nerve
radial nerve, tendon of biceps brachii, brachial artery, median nerve

questions.q: Why is the median cubital vein in the superficial fascia over the cubital fossa commonly chosen for venipuncture?
options: It is relatively superficial, prominent, and lies over the bicipital aponeurosis which helps shield the deeper brachial artery and median nerve
It contains oxygenated arterial blood at high pressure
It runs directly inside the radial canal
It has no anastomoses with deep or superficial veins
questions.explain: The median cubital vein bridges the cephalic and basilic veins superficially over the cubital fossa, and the underlying bicipital aponeurosis provides a protective barrier between it and the deeper brachial artery and median nerve.

open.q: Why is the median cubital vein frequently used for venipuncture at the elbow?
accept: it is superficial and separated from the brachial artery and median nerve by the bicipital aponeurosis
superficial location with bicipital aponeurosis protecting deeper vessels and nerve
accessible superficial position over the bicipital aponeurosis
superficial vein shielded from deeper artery and nerve by the bicipital aponeurosis

questions.q: A patient has a mid-shaft fracture of the humerus and presents with inability to extend the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints (wrist drop) with sensory loss over the dorsolateral hand. Which nerve is injured?
questions.explain: Radial nerve injury at or above the elbow paralyzes posterior forearm extensors of the wrist and fingers, producing wrist drop, and causes sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand/first web space.

open.q: Injury to which nerve causes wrist drop and loss of extension at the wrist and fingers?

questions.q: Which nerve innervates flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus in the anterior forearm?
questions.explain: While most anterior forearm flexors are innervated by the median nerve, flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar (medial) half of flexor digitorum profundus are supplied by the ulnar nerve.

open.q: Which nerve innervates flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus?

questions.q: Which muscle in the anterior forearm acts as a pronator of the forearm and arises from both a humeral head and an ulnar head?
questions.explain: Pronator teres has humeral and ulnar heads (with the median nerve passing between them) and inserts onto the lateral radius to pronate and weakly flex the forearm.

open.q: Which forearm muscle has humeral and ulnar heads and pronates the forearm?

questions.q: Which nerve branch supplies motor innervation to the deep extensor muscles of the posterior forearm (such as extensor digitorum and extensor pollicis longus) after passing through supinator?
questions.explain: The posterior interosseous nerve is the motor continuation of the deep branch of the radial nerve after it passes through supinator, innervating posterior forearm extensors without carrying cutaneous sensory fibers to the hand.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the posterior forearm extensor muscles after passing through supinator?

questions.q: Which nerve branch in the anterior forearm innervates flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus?
questions.explain: The anterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor branch of the median nerve in the forearm that runs along the anterior interosseous membrane to supply flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus.

open.q: Which branch of the median nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus and pronator quadratus?

questions.q: A patient cannot flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb or the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger when asked to make an OK sign, yet sensation in the median nerve palm is intact. Which nerve is affected?
questions.explain: Anterior interosseous nerve lesion selectively weakens flexor pollicis longus (thumb IP flexion) and lateral flexor digitorum profundus (index DIP flexion) plus pronator quadratus, sparing palmar cutaneous sensation because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel.

open.q: Loss of thumb interphalangeal and index distal interphalangeal flexion with spared palmar sensation points to a lesion of which nerve?

questions.q: Which muscle forms the lateral border of the cubital fossa and flexes the elbow most effectively when the forearm is in the mid-prone position?
questions.explain: Brachioradialis originates on the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts on the distal radius, forming the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa and acting as an elbow flexor in mid-pronation despite being innervated by the radial nerve.

open.q: Which radial-innervated muscle forms the lateral border of the cubital fossa and flexes the mid-prone forearm?

questions.q: What fibrous band bridges the radial and ulnar sides of the carpus anteriorly to convert the carpal arch into the carpal tunnel?
questions.explain: The flexor retinaculum spans from the scaphoid and trapezium laterally to the pisiform and hook of hamate medially, forming the roof of the carpal tunnel through which the median nerve and flexor tendons pass.

open.q: What structure forms the roof of the carpal tunnel across the anterior wrist?

questions.q: Why is palmar sensation over the thenar eminence typically preserved in classic carpal tunnel syndrome?
options: The thenar skin is supplied by the radial nerve
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
The ulnar nerve supplies the entire palmar surface of the thumb
The carpal tunnel contains no sensory fibers
questions.explain: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve branches off proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum, bypassing compression inside the carpal tunnel and preserving sensation over the central/thenar palm.

open.q: Why does carpal tunnel syndrome usually spare sensation over the central/thenar palm?
accept: the palmar cutaneous branch runs superficial to the flexor retinaculum
palmar cutaneous branch bypasses the carpal tunnel
palmar cutaneous branch is superficial to the retinaculum
sensation is carried by a branch outside the carpal tunnel

questions.q: Which tendons pass through the carpal tunnel alongside the median nerve?
options: Flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor digitorum profundus, and flexor pollicis longus tendons
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons
questions.explain: Nine flexor tendons—four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus, and one of flexor pollicis longus—pass through the carpal tunnel together with the median nerve. Flexor carpi radialis has its own canal.

open.q: Which flexor tendons travel through the carpal tunnel with the median nerve?
accept: flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor digitorum profundus, and flexor pollicis longus

questions.q: Which artery can be palpated on the lateral anterior wrist just lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis?
questions.explain: The radial artery lies superficially on the distal radius lateral to flexor carpi radialis tendon, making it the standard site for palpating the radial pulse and obtaining arterial blood gas or catheter access.

open.q: Which artery is palpated at the lateral wrist just lateral to flexor carpi radialis?

questions.q: Which two tendons form the lateral (radial) boundary of the anatomical snuffbox at the base of the thumb?
options: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis
Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus
Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris
questions.explain: The anatomical snuffbox is bounded laterally by tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, and medially by extensor pollicis longus. The radial artery crosses its floor, and the scaphoid lies deep in it.

open.q: Which two tendons form the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox?
accept: abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis

questions.q: Which group of intrinsic hand muscles forms the fleshy prominence at the base of the thumb and enables opposition?
questions.explain: The thenar eminence comprises abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and flexor pollicis brevis, enabling abduction, opposition, and flexion of the thumb; they are typically supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.

open.q: Which group of hand muscles forms the thenar eminence at the base of the thumb?

questions.q: What are the actions of the palmar interossei of the hand relative to the axial line of the middle finger?
options: Adduct the digits toward the middle finger
questions.explain: Using the PAD and DAB mnemonic, palmar interossei (PAD) adduct the fingers toward the axis of the middle finger, while dorsal interossei (DAB) abduct the fingers away from that axis.

open.q: What movement do the palmar interossei produce in the fingers?

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the vast majority of intrinsic hand muscles, including the hypothenar muscles, interossei, adductor pollicis, and medial two lumbricals?
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles, all palmar and dorsal interossei, adductor pollicis, and the third and fourth (medial two) lumbricals. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles and first two (lateral two) lumbricals.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the interossei, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, and medial two lumbricals?

questions.q: How do the lumbrical muscles of the hand affect joint positions of the fingers?
options: They flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints
They extend the metacarpophalangeal joints while flexing the interphalangeal joints
They insert exclusively onto the pisiform
questions.explain: Lumbricals arise from flexor digitorum profundus tendons and insert into the extensor expansions on the dorsal aspect of the proximal phalanges, enabling flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints combined with extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints.

open.q: What combined movement do the lumbricals produce at the finger joints?
accept: flexion at metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at interphalangeal joints
flex mcp joints and extend ip joints

questions.q: A patient has a lesion of the ulnar nerve at the elbow or wrist and cannot adduct the little finger or adduct the thumb firmly against the index finger (Froment sign). Which muscle primarily adducts the thumb?
questions.explain: Adductor pollicis adducts the thumb toward the palm/index finger and is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Paralysis causes weak pinch/adduction, often compensated by flexor pollicis longus (Froment sign).

open.q: Which ulnar-innervated muscle adducts the thumb and is tested when checking for Froment sign?

questions.q: Which joint is the only synovial articulation between the axial skeleton and the upper limb girdle?
questions.explain: The sternoclavicular joint connects the sternal end of the clavicle, the manubrium of the sternum, and the first costal cartilage, serving as the sole synovial linkage between the upper limb skeleton and axial skeleton.

open.q: Which joint is the sole synovial connection between the upper limb girdle and the axial skeleton?

questions.q: Which fibrocartilaginous structure deepens the shallow glenoid cavity of the scapula at the shoulder joint?
questions.explain: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached around the margin of the glenoid cavity that deepens the socket slightly and increases contact area with the humeral head.

open.q: What fibrocartilaginous rim deepens the glenoid cavity of the shoulder joint?

questions.q: What is the function of the annular ligament of the radius at the proximal radioulnar joint?
options: It holds the head of the radius against the radial notch of the ulna while allowing rotation
It locks the elbow in full extension
It prevents all pronation and supination
It connects the clavicle to the coracoid process
questions.explain: The annular ligament forms a strong fibrous collar around the head of the radius attached to the ulna, keeping the radial head within the radial notch during pronation and supination. In young children, traction can pull the radial head partially out of it (pulled elbow).

open.q: How does the annular ligament stabilize the head of the radius during forearm rotation?
accept: it encircles the radial head against the radial notch of the ulna while permitting rotation
holds the head of the radius in the radial notch so it can rotate
collars the radial head against the ulna
keeps the radial head in place during pronation and supination

questions.q: Which movement occurs at the radioulnar joints when the palm turns anteriorly (from anatomical position/supination) or posteriorly?
questions.explain: The proximal and distal radioulnar joints allow the radius to pivot around the ulna, producing pronation (turning palm posteriorly/downward) and supination (turning palm anteriorly/upward).

open.q: Which movements of the forearm take place at the radioulnar joints?

questions.q: At which anatomical landmark does the subclavian artery become the axillary artery?
options: Lateral border of the first rib
questions.explain: The subclavian artery continues as the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib, and the axillary artery continues as the brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major.

open.q: At which landmark does the subclavian artery transition into the axillary artery?
accept: lateral border of the first rib

questions.q: Along which side of the upper limb does the cephalic vein ascend before piercing the clavipectoral fascia to drain into the axillary vein?
questions.explain: The cephalic vein arises from the lateral side of the dorsal venous network of the hand, ascends along the lateral/anterolateral forearm and arm in the deltopectoral groove, and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein.

open.q: Along which aspect of the upper limb does the cephalic vein ascend before joining the axillary vein?

questions.q: Where does the basilic vein pierce the deep fascia of the arm to join the brachial veins and form the axillary vein?
options: Near the middle of the medial arm
questions.explain: The basilic vein ascends along the medial aspect of the forearm and lower arm superficially, then pierces the brachial fascia around mid-arm to join the brachial (vena comitans) veins and form the axillary vein.

open.q: Around which region of the arm does the basilic vein pierce the deep fascia?
accept: middle of the arm on the medial side

questions.q: Which arterial arch in the palm is formed primarily as the direct continuation of the ulnar artery anastomosing with the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery?
questions.explain: The superficial palmar arch lies deep to the palmar aponeurosis and is formed mainly by the ulnar artery with a contribution from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery, giving off common palmar digital arteries.

open.q: Which palmar arterial arch is formed mainly by the ulnar artery?

questions.q: How is the deep palmar arch in the hand primarily formed?
options: By the radial artery anastomosing with the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery
By the musculocutaneous and axillary arteries
By the thoracoacromial and suprascapular arteries
questions.explain: The deep palmar arch lies across the bases of the metacarpals and is formed primarily by the terminal radial artery joining the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery, giving off princeps pollicis, radialis indicis, and palmar metacarpal arteries.

open.q: Which arteries join to form the deep palmar arch of the hand?
accept: radial artery and deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery
terminal radial artery with deep branch of ulnar artery

questions.q: A patient has a supracondylar fracture of the humerus with severe anterior displacement of the distal fragment, threatening the brachial artery and median nerve. What ischemic complication of the forearm can follow untreated brachial artery injury?
questions.explain: Ischemia and compartment swelling in the anterior forearm after brachial artery injury or supracondylar humeral fracture can cause muscle and nerve necrosis followed by fibrous shortening, known as Volkmann ischemic contracture.

open.q: What forearm contracture can result from untreated ischemia after brachial artery injury or supracondylar humeral fracture?
